source: q-0009 routing: feasibility of a module-disjoint WITHIN-DEEP eval split
INTERPRETATION: A module-disjoint within-deep split is FEASIBLE and not leakage-prone by construction: the 633 targets span 452 modules with no module above 0.9% of targets, so an area-stratified every-5th-module holdout cleanly partitions them into 502 train / 131 eval targets (82 eval modules), with NO module on both sides and all 17/23 areas represented on each. Projecting e-0028's per-area yield gives ~442.2 verified train frontiers (AMPLE) and ~115.8 verified eval frontiers (>= the ~30 needed to score pass@k). So e-0029's MARGINAL ~126 verdict is SPECIFIC to insisting on miniF2F transfer: the within-deep route (e-0029's option a) restores an AMPLE training band (~442.2 vs 300) with a leakage-controlled held-out eval — at the cost of measuring the granularity/planner effect on the deep distribution itself, not on competition math. This routes the Modal go/no-go: option (a) is the cheap, supply-ample path; the only residual cost is the external-validity narrowing (deep eval, not miniF2F).
CAVEAT: Module-disjoint is the standard, defensible leakage control for a proof corpus (build_sft.py uses module-stratified splits) but it is not airtight: two decls in DIFFERENT modules can still share a frontier lemma, so a residual cross-module leakage is possible and would need a lemma-overlap audit at verify time. Verified counts are the e-0028 per-area projection, not an actual round-trip (needs the Modal pass); this projects COUNTS not pass@k. Bands are chain anchors (e-0014 ~850 'ample', e-0029 ~100 floor), not a measured SFT learning curve.
